article.headline: Flipbook Envisions a Web Built Entirely on AI-Generated Pixels
article.lede: On April 23, 2026, a three-person team unveiled **Flipbook**, a prototype that discards the web's entire rendering stack—HTML, CSS, the layout engine—and replaces it with a generative video model that draws every visible pixel on demand. The result is an interface where clicking a landmark on a travel page reshapes the whole canvas into a new illustrated scene, with no underlying document model, no selectable text, and no fixed buttons. Whether this represents a glimpse of a post-browser future or a compelling dead end is the question it forces.
article.body:
Zain Shah, a former researcher at OpenAI and a Y Combinator alumnus, Eddie Jiao, previously at AI hardware start-up Humane, and Drew O'Carr, formerly of Apple (AAPL), built **Flipbook** and released it to the public on April 23, 2026. The premise is sweeping: replace the web browser's conventional document model with a continuous stream of AI-generated images. Every label, map, button, and paragraph visible on screen is drawn pixel by pixel by a neural network. There is no Document Object Model, no HTML tree, no rendered text—just canvas.

The default experience is more measured than the launch announcement suggests. When a user submits a query, the backend runs an image-generation pipeline that delivers results as a *progressive JPEG*—an encoding that transmits from low to high resolution so a blurry version appears immediately and sharpens as data arrives—streamed over *Server-Sent Events* (a protocol for one-directional server-to-browser pushes), taking roughly nineteen seconds per page. Each finished image acquires a stable URL and forms one node in a navigable graph. The genuinely novel mechanism arrives on click: coordinates are sent to a *vision-language model*, a neural network that reasons jointly across text and images, which infers what the user meant to interact with and uses that inference as the prompt for the next generated image. There are no predefined links or buttons; navigation is entirely inferential. The "live 1080p 24fps video stream" promoted in the announcement is an opt-in mode requiring high-end H100 GPU hardware and is disabled by default.

The image generation runs on **LTX-Video**, an open-source *Diffusion Transformer* model developed by Lightricks, an Israeli creative software company best known for consumer editing apps including Facetune and Videoleap. Diffusion Transformers (*DiT*) replace the *U-Net* backbone used in earlier diffusion models—a convolutional architecture shaped like the letter U—with a pure Transformer that attends globally across the full spatial-temporal sequence. Flipbook uses the 2B distilled variant of LTX-Video, which reduces the denoising process from roughly fifty steps to as few as eight, achieving speeds approximately fifteen times faster than the non-distilled model. Inference runs on Modal Labs, a serverless GPU cloud that bills only for compute actually consumed. Even so, launch-day demand overwhelmed the team's credits within hours, and Modal stepped in as a compute sponsor before the queue reached two hours.

Flipbook arrives at a contested moment in the design of AI-native software. Andrej Karpathy, in an April 2026 lecture, framed a vision he called *Software 3.0*—computation driven by large language models as interpreters of natural language—and extrapolated toward interfaces rendered entirely by diffusion models. Flipbook is a working, if rough, prototype of the most radical version of that idea. The dominant industry approach takes a different path: Alphabet (GOOGL) has proposed *A2UI*, an open standard in which AI agents compose interfaces from JSON-declared component catalogs that clients render natively; Vercel's *Generative UI* tooling generates React components via model tool calls; and Anthropic's *Claude Artifacts* produces live HTML and JavaScript in a sandboxed frame. These structured approaches preserve accessibility, semantic text, keyboard navigation, and hyperlinking—capabilities Flipbook's pixel-native canvas cannot offer, since every character is a drawn glyph invisible to screen readers.

The team describes Flipbook explicitly as a prototype. Text rendering remains unreliable, as diffusion models have long struggled to accurately form letters at pixel level. There is no persistent application state: each click regenerates from scratch rather than updating a live document. Within days of launch, an independent reimplementation named *openflipbook* appeared and found the component technologies—*VLM*-based click resolution, progressive image delivery over *SSE*, fMP4 segment playback via the browser's *Media Source Extensions* API—to be commercially available and unremarkable in isolation. What Flipbook assembles is a specific composition of these parts around a provocative thesis: that the right abstraction for future computing may not be a document model at all, but **an infinite canvas whose contents are grown from intention rather than authored in advance**.

concepts.definition: A browser protocol that keeps a one-directional connection open from server to client, pushing data as it becomes available without the client needing to poll. Commonly used for streaming text or binary chunks incrementally—in Flipbook's case, progressive JPEG image data as the model refines its output.

A neural network trained to reason jointly over images and text. In Flipbook, a VLM receives the current page image plus the pixel coordinates of the user's click and infers a semantic description of what was clicked—'the Eiffel Tower', 'a ticket price'—which then becomes the prompt for the next generated image.

An architecture for image or video generation that replaces the U-Net backbone of earlier diffusion models with a pure Transformer. The Transformer attends globally across the full spatial and temporal sequence, generally producing more coherent outputs. LTX-Video, which Flipbook uses, is a prominent example.

A convolutional neural network architecture shaped like the letter U, widely used as the denoising backbone in earlier diffusion-based image generators such as Stable Diffusion. In image and video generation, DiT architectures have largely superseded it.

A conceptual framework articulated by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy in which Software 1.0 is explicit human-written code, Software 2.0 is neural networks trained on data, and Software 3.0 is prompts—programs written in natural language and interpreted by large language models at runtime. Karpathy has extrapolated the idea to interfaces rendered entirely by generative models.

An open standard proposed by Alphabet's Google in 2026 for agent-driven interfaces. Rather than generating raw pixels or arbitrary code, AI agents compose interfaces by selecting from a catalog of pre-declared JSON components that host applications render natively, preserving accessibility, security, and semantic structure.

A pattern in which a language model produces structured user-interface components—React elements, JSON schemas, or HTML—in response to user input, rather than generating static text. The model's output is rendered live by the client framework. Contrasted with Flipbook's approach of generating raw pixels rather than structured layout primitives.

A browser API that lets JavaScript feed compressed video segments into a native video element in real time, enabling adaptive streaming without a dedicated plugin. Flipbook's opt-in video mode uses MSE to splice incoming fMP4 (fragmented MP4) chunks into a live video canvas as they arrive from Modal Labs GPUs.

A JPEG encoding that transmits the image in multiple passes from low to high resolution, letting the viewer see a blurry approximation immediately that sharpens as more data arrives. Flipbook's default mode delivers each generated page this way over SSE, taking roughly nineteen seconds for the full image.

repos.summary: The official open-source repository for LTX-Video, Lightricks's Diffusion Transformer model for real-time video generation. The 2B distilled variant achieves roughly fifteen times faster inference than the non-distilled model, making near-real-time generation feasible on high-end GPUs. Licensed under Apache 2.0 for commercial use by companies under $10M ARR.

An open-source reimplementation of Flipbook that appeared within days of the original launch, built by reverse-engineering Flipbook's network traffic. It replicates the core loop—VLM click resolution, progressive SSE image delivery, and MSE-based video streaming—using publicly available APIs. The accompanying STORY.md is a detailed technical post-mortem of how the original system actually works versus how it was marketed.

article.fact_check: The announcement thread's central phrase—'streamed live directly from a model'—overstates the default experience. In normal operation, Flipbook generates a progressive JPEG over Server-Sent Events taking roughly nineteen seconds per page; it is not a live stream. True 1080p 24fps video streaming is an opt-in mode disabled by default because it requires high-end H100 GPUs at significant cost. The claim that there is 'no code' is accurate with respect to layout and content—there is no HTML tree describing the page—but the browser still runs substantial JavaScript to handle WebSocket connections, MSE playback, and click-coordinate handling. These are meaningful nuances rather than outright falsehoods, but the promotional framing collapses a spectrum of technical realities into a single vivid claim.
article.thread_summary: Shah's five-tweet thread announced Flipbook, demonstrated it with a Paris travel-planning example, and tagged infrastructure partners LTX Studio and Modal Labs. In tweet 4/5, Shah acknowledged current limitations—Flipbook is today optimized for visual explanations—and sketched a vision for expanding the approach to more structured use cases, including coding interfaces, as models become more accurate and stateful. A follow-up post expressed surprise at the scale of public response and thanked Modal for providing additional compute after launch-day demand exhausted the team's own credits within hours.

ticker_aapl.name: Apple Inc.
ticker_aapl.blurb: Apple designs and markets consumer electronics (iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch), software, and digital services. The iPhone remains the dominant revenue driver, but the Services segment — comprising the App Store, Apple Music, iCloud, Apple Pay, and licensing — has grown into a high-margin business that Wall Street values separately. Apple commands one of the highest brand loyalty rates in consumer technology and operates a tightly integrated hardware-software ecosystem.
ticker_aapl.recent: Apple reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $400 billion. The company has faced headwinds from slowing iPhone upgrade cycles in mature markets and regulatory pressure on App Store commissions in both the US and EU. Apple Intelligence, its generative AI suite, launched in late 2024 but has not yet materially re-accelerated upgrade cycles. Paul Pelosi sold 45,000 shares of AAPL according to the January 2026 PTR disclosure — the largest single sale in the filing by share count.

ticker_googl.name: Alphabet Inc. (Class A)
ticker_googl.blurb: Alphabet is the parent company of Google, the world's dominant search engine, as well as YouTube, the Google Cloud Platform, and a portfolio of moonshot bets (Waymo, DeepMind, Verily). Search advertising accounts for the majority of revenue, but the cloud division has grown into a multi-billion-dollar profit centre. Alphabet is also a leading player in generative AI, having developed the Gemini family of large language models and integrated them across its product suite.
ticker_googl.recent: Alphabet reported FY2025 revenue of approximately $370 billion, with Google Cloud crossing $50 billion annually. The company has faced antitrust scrutiny in both the US and EU, with a US federal court ruling in 2024 that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search. Despite regulatory headwinds, the stock has benefited from AI-driven search enhancements and strong cloud growth. Paul Pelosi exercised call options with a $150 strike (purchased January 2025, exercised January 2026) gaining approximately 75% over the period.
